cells.tense: The steady pull toward what you want is here now, with the pen in your hand.
cells.act: use the finished thing for an hour instead of improving it
cells.ask: Take something finished that came from what you wanted and use it just as it is, changing nothing to make it better.
cells.core:
What draws you forward isn't borrowed from anyone, and something built out of an earlier version of it is already sitting here, done. You can use that thing as it stands. The satisfaction of it is available while you still hold the pen on the next one, and using it doesn't ask you to stop wanting more.

The balance holds through stretches where nothing gets improved. Pick the thing that was really made — the plan that got run, the room that got set up, the work that went out — and use it the way anyone else would. That's the act: use the finished thing for an hour instead of improving it. The pull keeps going without your help.
cells.sheetLine: The built thing can be used before it's improved.
cells.verb: align steady pull with what you want
cells.place: the place inside where wanting points at what's worth heading for

cells.tense: At this speed the pull has already reached a place it hasn't arrived at, and it braces there.
cells.act: gather the scattered thoughts into one line
cells.ask: Put every thought about where you're headed on one page, draw a single line through it in order, and work from that line for the rest of the week.
cells.core:
Pull toward what's bright, lived too far forward, turns into steering from a place you haven't actually reached. The next stretch gets decided from a future that isn't written yet. Reach gets called readiness. The direction is locked before the feeling has its say.

A remedy is already in how you think. Gather the scattered thoughts into one line before you act: open a page, put down everything tugging at you about where you're headed — no order, no fixing — then shape the pieces into one line you can act on. That isn't less desire. It's desire getting something solid to stand on. That's the act: gather the scattered thoughts into one line.
cells.sheetLine: You're living where you're headed before you get there.

cells.tense: What you were drawn toward is behind you, and you're still standing at that door.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: List five things one finished chapter in your life produced, and read the list once without aiming it at anything ahead.
cells.core:
The pull you steered by has set, and the ambition it carried still points at where you were. Something in the present gets treated as a waypoint on a road that stopped. Desire has gone quiet behind a door already closed.

What the ending left is still here, and it isn't only absence. Set aside an hour and count what that chapter actually produced: work, a skill, a way you now handle things, people who came from it. Look at the yield rather than the loss. That's the act: count what the ending gave you. The pull doesn't need relighting tonight; it needs somewhere to stand while you count.
cells.sheetLine: It ended. What it left you is still here.

cells.tense: You're steering by an aim you keep saying you didn't choose.
cells.act: commit to the long build and do today's part
cells.ask: Keep the build you're drawn toward going with steady daily work, do the small part that's today's, and stop calling the progress accidental.
cells.core:
Somewhere in the middle of ordinary life, a direction is being lived. The pull is running, and whoever's at the wheel says it wasn't decided — no route is being read, only motion. The steering is real. It just isn't being owned.

A long build is what's already happening, with no announcement and nothing to name yet. Set the next piece of it in front of yourself and do that, at a size you can actually hold. That's the act: commit to the long build and do today's part. The direction you say you didn't choose is made by the days you show up for. Own one of those days and the talk starts to change.
cells.sheetLine: The aim you say you didn't choose runs on your days.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft is that the person used to have steady pull toward what they wanted before something ended; the record only supports that the seat is running on empty now. A reader could reasonably say the emptiness is new, or comes from something other than an ending, and my read would be wrong. The ask survives that: counting what a finished change actually produced needs no claim about what happened or how long ago. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is waiting inside the Too Little cell, where 'nobody's asking you to conjure a new star' is my coinage; it stays in the author's drawer and never reaches glass.
